title: Generate–Verify–Repair for Intent‑Driven Network Changes: Controlled Evaluation with a Deterministic Verifier
abstract: We evaluate whether a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipeline—single‑shot LLM generation followed by a deterministic network verifier and up to one automated repair—reduces accepted unsafe network changes versus LLM‑only generation on a standardized synthetic NetOps intent workload. In a preregistered paired design (study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29) we ran N=500 distinct synthetic intents (shared single initial candidate per intent) with generation by gpt-5-mini and adjudication by a deterministic verifier. Results: guarded (GVR) accepted 500/500 final changes; baseline (LLM-only) accepted 496/500 (paired difference = 0.008). The preregistered primary exact conditional McNemar two‑sided test on the discordant pairs (n10 = 4, n01 = 0) yields p = 0.125 computed as p = 2 * PBinom(X ≥ 4; n = 4, p = 0.5). An exploratory paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.002, 0.016]; the bootstrap interval was predeclared exploratory and is interpreted cautiously given the small number of discordant pairs. Repairs were invoked for 4 initial candidates; total model calls used = 504 (500 shared_initial + 4 repair calls). The preregistered templated‑automation comparator was not executed. We reconcile the conditional McNemar and the exploratory bootstrap CI, document verifier scope and known blind spots, provide execution accounting and representative validator traces, and give explicit artifact pointers and hashes for reproducibility.

sections.introduction: Translating operator intent to device configuration is a promising application of large language models (LLMs) in network operations (NetOps), but operational deployment is hindered by hallucinations and factual errors that can produce unsafe transient states or incorrect CLI sequences. A practical mitigation architecture is generate–verify–repair (GVR): generate a candidate configuration with an LLM, deterministically verify it against encoded workflow and policy rules, and, if verification fails, attempt a bounded automated repair. We evaluate whether a GVR pipeline with a single deterministic verifier and at most one automated repair reduces the rate of accepted unsafe changes compared to LLM‑only generation on a standardized synthetic workload. Our contributions are (1) a preregistered paired trial (N=500 intents) with full archived artifacts; (2) a detailed, artifact-grounded description of generation, verifier semantics, and the bounded repair loop; (3) reconciled confirmatory inference (two‑sided conditional exact McNemar) and exploratory bootstrap interval reporting with an explicit small‑discordant caveat; and (4) execution accounting, representative validator traces, and a discussion of verifier blind spots and operational limits.
sections.related_work: Three literatures motivate this study. Surveys and system papers document active work on LLM‑assisted NetOps (intent translation, configuration generation, AIOps, and multi‑agent orchestration) and emphasize hallucination as a deployment barrier. Methodological work on tool‑augmented LLMs, retrieval‑augmented generation (RAG), and generate–validate–repair architectures stresses standardized evaluation and the need to quantify verifier coverage and cost. Deterministic configuration verifiers and analyzers (Batfish‑style tools and distributed verifiers) provide operationally useful oracles for many syntactic and workflow properties, but prior empirical evaluations seldom combine preregistration, paired designs, and full archival artifacts at the scale used here. Our experiment situates itself at the intersection by using a deterministic verifier as the operational adjudicator and a bounded repair policy under a preregistered confirmatory plan.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design: The study was preregistered as study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29 (preregistration SHA‑256 = aa8982a27c73e51521ac023a78adcfa358ef3978c0f9bc05213801fcbd2f1d0a) with a paired confirmatory design. Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline across N = 500 distinct intents stratified evenly across 10 synthetic topology profiles (50 intents per profile). Sampling seeds, the deterministic task generator, and the analysis executor were frozen before execution. Planned sample size and power targeted an absolute paired increase of ≈0.08; realized margins produced fewer discordants than expected (see Results). Tasks and expected_final_state entries derive from synthetic_topologies_v1 and synthetic_device_configs_v1.
Generation and orchestration: For each intent a single shared_initial_generation candidate was produced by gpt-5-mini (declared_model_version recorded in execution/model_configuration.json; execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 = a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820). The GVR controller validated the shared candidate with deterministic_netops_validator_v5. If verification failed, the controller issued at most one automated repair call (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1) using a constrained repair prompt template that included the intent abstraction and verifier violation codes; a repair candidate was accepted only if the verifier returned valid=true. The baseline condition accepted the shared candidate without repair. Provider‑call accounting (deterministic_reconciliation.json) records hosted_model_call_event_count = 504 and stage_counts mapping shared_initial_generation = 500, repair = 4, consistent with the model_call budget specified in the preregistration.
Deterministic verifier semantics: The primary verifier implements a fixed deterministic pipeline on normalized CLI sequences: (i) syntactic parsing and normalization to canonical command forms; (ii) workflow and required‑sequence checks (patterns such as must_be_down_for_fields and all_down_before_any_field_change); (iii) availability/group constraints (exactly_active and minimum_active_in_groups); (iv) dependency and paired‑field enforcement (paired MTU changes, equal_final_fields); and (v) final‑state comparison against the task expected_final_state. Any nonempty violation set yields a failing outcome. For each episode the verifier emits normalized_configuration, observed_touched_field_count, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation list, and boolean valid. The verifier implementation identifier is deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and the human‑readable verifier codebook (violation‑code → short description) is enumerated in the archived execution manifest; the execution manifest lists the exact artifact path and SHA for the codebook (see execution/execution_manifest.json in the evidence bundle for that manifest entry). Representative validator_trace JSON objects are archived under execution/scoring/ and include the emitted fields described above.
Statistical plan and tests: The preregistered confirmatory test is the two‑sided conditional exact McNemar on discordant pairs. In the conditional formulation let n = n10 + n01 be the number of discordant pairs and k = n10 the count favoring GVR; the two‑sided exact p‑value is p = 2 * sum_{x=k}^{n} Binom(n,x) * 0.5^{n}. The paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (exploratory) was predeclared with bootstrap_resamples = 10,000 and bootstrap_seed = 1729. Primary analysis uses complete pairs (no imputation) per preregistration; missingness and technical‑failure handling are described in the preregistration and execution manifest.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and primary counts: The run completed completed_episode_count = 1000 (500 intents × 2 conditions) with model_calls_used = 504 (provider audit: hosted_model_call_event_count = 504, completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 504, failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 0; cache_hit_count = 0). analysis/condition_summary.csv reports baseline successes 496/500 (0.992) and guarded successes 500/500 (1.000). The paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is n11 = 496, n10 = 4, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Repairs were invoked for four initial candidates; all four repair attempts produced verifier‑passing outcomes and correspond to the four discordant pairs (n10 = 4). Mean model calls per accepted change ≈ 504/500 = 1.008.
Confirmatory exact McNemar calculation: Observed discordants n = n10 + n01 = 4 with k = n10 = 4. Using the conditional exact formulation the two‑sided p‑value is p = 2 * PBinom(X ≥ 4; n = 4, p = 0.5). For n = 4, PBinom(X ≥ 4; n = 4, p = 0.5) = 1/16, hence p = 2 * (1/16) = 0.125. Because this exact conditional test was the preregistered decision rule we do not claim confirmatory statistical significance for the primary estimand.
Exploratory paired bootstrap interval: The preregistered exploratory paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) for the paired difference is [0.002, 0.016] (artifact: analysis/paired_difference_figure.svg and analysis/analysis_log.jsonl). The bootstrap procedure resampled paired outcomes (not conditioning on margins) and produced the percentile CI reported here; the bootstrap was predeclared exploratory and is interpreted with the small‑discordant caveat (see Discussion).
Representative episode diagnostics: Representative scoring JSON objects (execution/scoring/task-00000*-*.json) include verifier_trace entries with validation_before and validation_after objects, normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_count, and validator_version = 5.0. Example difficulty patterns exercised include shutdown_configure_restore, make_before_break_uplink_switchover, and paired_link_atomic_mtu_change. The four repaired episodes show verifier‑detectable sequence or availability violations that a single constrained repair prompt corrected; repair prompts included the verifier violation codes and the intent abstraction and are archived in provider traces.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation of inferential outcomes: The GVR pipeline prevented four verifier‑detectable unsafe initial candidates that baseline would have accepted; the paired difference is 0.008. Under the preregistered conditional exact McNemar (p = 0.125) this difference is not confirmatory. The exploratory bootstrap CI excludes zero but must be interpreted cautiously: the conditional McNemar conditions on observed margins and evaluates the binomial tail of discordant outcomes; with n = 4 and k = 4 this yields p = 0.125. The paired bootstrap resamples pairs without fixing margins and can produce a nonzero lower CI bound when most pairs are concordant and a small number are discordant. Because the bootstrap was predeclared exploratory we present both inferential perspectives and follow the preregistered decision rule for the primary claim.
Verifier coverage and blind spots: The deterministic verifier enforces canonical normalization, required sequencing, availability/group constraints, dependency and paired‑field rules, and final‑state equality to task expected_final_state. It does not model vendor‑specific CLI semantics, control‑plane timing/convergence, vendor idiosyncrasies, hardware resource limits, or out‑of‑band side effects. Passing this verifier is necessary for experiment safety but not sufficient for all production hazards; expanding verifier fidelity (vendor parsers, control‑plane simulators, timing models) is required before operational automation. The human‑readable verifier codebook (violation‑code → description) is enumerated in the archived execution manifest; the manifest records the exact codebook artifact path and SHA (see execution/execution_manifest.json in the evidence bundle).
Operational implications and cost tradeoffs: A compact deterministic verifier plus a bounded repair loop intercepted verifier‑detectable hazards at low LLM overhead in this synthetic workload. The observed low repair rate (4/500) implies modest model overhead for this task set; mean model calls per accepted change ≈ 1.008. Production workloads with higher hallucination or adversarial inputs would change the cost/benefit calculus: repair frequency, verifier runtime, and tool‑orchestration latency determine whether GVR is operationally practical. Deterministic_reconciliation.json records stage_counts and provider audit fields that permit downstream per‑task latency/cost accounting from archived traces.
Threats to validity: Internal validity is strong due to preregistration, paired design, fixed seeds, and complete pairs (complete_pair_count = 500). Construct validity is limited by synthetic device templates and the verifier abstraction (synthetic_topologies_v1, synthetic_device_configs_v1, deterministic_netops_validator_v5). External validity is constrained by single‑model scope (gpt-5-mini) and synthetic topologies; multi‑model replication and vendor‑specific real‑device tests remain future work. Conclusion validity: the preregistered power plan assumed larger discordance (targeted effect ≈ 0.08); the realized near‑ceiling baseline (0.992) yielded only four discordant pairs, reducing realized power versus the preregistered assumption and limiting confirmatory sensitivity. All of these limitations are recorded in the archived manifests and analysis artifacts.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired trial (N = 500) using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic verifier, a generate–verify–repair pipeline repaired four verifier‑detectable unsafe initial candidates at modest model‑call cost (4 repairs; model_calls_used = 504). The paired difference = 0.008 yields an exploratory bootstrap 95% CI [0.002, 0.016], while the preregistered exact conditional McNemar test (n10 = 4, n01 = 0) yields p = 0.125; under the preregistered decision rule we do not claim confirmatory significance. Deterministic verification plus a bounded repair loop can remove verifier‑detectable unsafe outputs with low overhead in synthetic settings; broader operational claims require expanded verifier fidelity, adversarial NetOps evaluation, multi‑model replication, and execution of the preregistered templated comparator (which was not executed here). All primary execution and analysis artifacts cited are archived in the evidence bundle for independent verification; key artifact hashes and manifest pointers are listed in the Disclosure Statement.

Preregistration: study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29 (preregistration SHA‑256 = aa8982a27c73e51521ac023a78adcfa358ef3978c0f9bc05213801fcbd2f1d0a). Representative artifact hashes included in the evidence bundle: execution/raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 = fe9b93ef5cc5a237a3361f18f45fabf14cd23a1c679556f65477f9f681915d02; execution/task_manifest.jsonl SHA‑256 = 5a822e787302a0b3bb03a86a81b20564a44e2636731f853f9d45ac12e4876cc8; analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 = 8fb135cec541cbe0b14f16125db33154a41460c49958427fe8e7f3e1f2abfece; analysis/analysis_log.jsonl SHA‑256 = 261ec80ea9343fccbcd0a62294f5382773770fd59d387dc9d749de50ca909b3e. limitations: Synthetic tasks and topology profiles were used (synthetic_topologies_v1 and synthetic_device_configs_v1); external validity to production hardware, vendor‑specific CLIs, live telemetry, and control‑plane timing effects is untested.
Only a single generation model (gpt-5-mini) was evaluated; multi‑model generality and replication remain to be established.

Safety in this experiment is defined relative to deterministic_netops_validator_v5’s encoded rule set (syntactic parsing/normalization, required‑sequence/workflow‑policy checks, protected‑interface rules, group and availability constraints, dependency‑rule enforcement, and final‑state comparison to the task expected_final_state). Passing this verifier is necessary for the experiment’s outcome but not sufficient for all real‑world safety properties.

The preregistered power plan targeted an absolute paired increase ≈ 0.08 (8 percentage points). The observed baseline success rate (496/500 = 0.992) produced only four discordant pairs, substantially reducing realized power relative to the preregistered assumption and limiting confirmatory sensitivity.

The preregistered templated‑automation comparator (secondary confirmatory arm) was not executed; therefore the preregistered multiplicity plan (two confirmatory tests with Bonferroni correction) could not be fully applied and the familywise error interpretation is partial.
